transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Well... I guess I'm here because of work. Things at the store. I'm a supervisor, so I have to... explain things. Like the inventory numbers, or the weekend schedule. But lately, when I try to do that, it just... comes out wrong. 

I start talking about the delivery trucks, and then somehow I'm talking about Thursdays, and then... I don't know, the grill at my church, and then how my boss sounded the other day. It all just gets jumbled up. People just... look at me. Like they have no idea what I'm talking about. So... that's why I'm here.
When did you first notice this problem with your speech becoming jumbled like this? Was it something that started recently, or has this been happening for a long time?
I suppose... maybe six months. Just... out on the sales floor. That's when it started getting noticeable, I guess. The... the jumbled parts, and when I just stop. About half a year now.
Besides the jumbled speech, have you noticed any changes in your memory, your ability to think clearly, or how you handle everyday tasks over these past six months?

Well... work has been hard. They... they don't let me run the weekend shifts anymore. Too busy, I guess. My boss... we had a review. He said I might get suspended if I don't... fix things. 

And at home... I don't know. My wife just does more now. The things I used to do. People just... they get uncomfortable around me. Or confused. So she just handles it instead. It's just... hard to manage things right now.
Over these past six months, have you noticed any problems with your memory—like forgetting things you usually remember, or having trouble keeping track of information?
Memory? I... I don't think so. I haven't really noticed anything like that. Just... what I told you before. The talking part. But remembering things... I think that's fine.

Before these past six months, going back to when you were younger—did you ever have any trouble speaking clearly, or did teachers or family ever mention problems with how you talked or put words together?
No. Nothing like that. Not... not when I was younger. Just... just recently. Like I said.
Have you had any recent illnesses, infections, high fevers, head injuries, or times when you felt confused or disoriented—even briefly—in the past six months?
No. I haven't been sick. No head injuries or... or fevers. Just... just what I've told you.
Have you ever lost consciousness, had a seizure, or had a period where you weren't aware of what was happening around you during these past six months?
No... I haven't passed out or anything. No seizures. I... I know what's going on around me. Just... no.
Has your ability to speak been getting worse over these six months, or has it stayed about the same since it started?
It's... it's just about the same, I guess. Hasn't really changed. Just... the same.
Have you noticed any changes in how you walk, your balance, your coordination, or any tremors or stiffness in your body over these past six months?
No... I walk fine. I haven't noticed any shaking or... anything like that. It's just normal.
When you're trying to explain something at work, do you have trouble finding the right words to use, or is it more that the words come out in the wrong order—like the sentences don't make sense?

I guess... it's more that they just jump around. Like, if I'm trying to explain the inventory numbers or the weekend schedule... I'll start talking about the trucks, and then... Thursdays. And then maybe the church grill, or my boss's tone. I don't know. People just look at me like they can't follow what I'm saying. That's mostly why I came in.
When you were in school as a child, did your teachers ever say anything about your reading, writing, or how you expressed yourself in class—even if you don't remember having problems yourself?
No, I don't... I don't remember anything like that. School was just school. No one said anything.
Besides the jumbled speech, have you noticed any difficulty with understanding what other people say to you, or any trouble with reading or writing over these past six months?
No... I understand what people say just fine. And reading and writing... I haven't had any trouble with that. It's really just... what I told you before.
Over these past six months, have you noticed any changes in how you think or reason through problems, or any new difficulty with things like planning your day or making decisions?
No... not really. I just do what I need to do at work. Decisions are fine. I haven't noticed any changes like that.

When you were growing up, did you ever feel like you had to work harder than other kids to keep up with conversations, or did anyone ever say you were a 'late talker' or had trouble with speech when you were very young—even if it seemed to improve?
No... I don't think so. My parents never mentioned anything like that. I talked fine, as far as I know.
When you were a child or teenager, did you ever need extra help in school with any subject, or did you ever attend any special classes or tutoring—even if it was just for a short time?
No. I didn't need any extra help. I did fine in school. Just regular classes.

I want to go back to something. When you were in your twenties or thirties, before these past six months, did anyone ever comment that you had an unusual way of speaking, or did you ever feel like organizing your thoughts into words was harder for you than it seemed to be for other people?
No... nobody ever said anything like that. I just talked normally. People understood me fine, as far as I know.

Has anyone in your family—parents, siblings, grandparents—ever been diagnosed with dementia, Alzheimer's disease, or any kind of neurological disease that affected their thinking or speech, especially if it started before age 65?
No... not that I'm aware of. Nobody had Alzheimer's or... anything like that. They just got older, I guess. Nothing unusual.

Looking back to when you were in elementary school, do you remember if reading out loud in class felt different or harder for you compared to other kids, or if you ever mixed up the order of words when you were writing?
No... I don't remember anything like that. Reading was... just reading. I didn't mix things up.

You mentioned this started about six months ago. Before that six-month period, going all the way back through your entire adult life—were you always able to speak clearly and organize your thoughts into words the way most people do, or is there any chance this problem has actually been there your whole life but you just didn't think of it as a problem until work made it noticeable?
No... it wasn't there my whole life. I've always been able to communicate just fine. It's... it's really only been lately. I never had a problem before this.
Have you noticed any difficulty finding your way to familiar places, or any trouble remembering people's names or faces that you used to know well over these past six months?
No... I haven't gotten lost or anything. I know my way around. And... I remember people just fine. That hasn't been a problem.

doctor.intent: Distinguish between a neurodegenerative disorder (G31.83 - Primary progressive aphasia) and a lifelong language disorder that only recently became problematic (F80.2 - Specific language disorder). The key differentiator is whether there is objective evidence of cognitive or neurological decline, particularly in executive function or other domains beyond speech, which would support a neurodegenerative process rather than a longstanding developmental disorder.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a 6-month history of progressive speech disorganization characterized by tangential, non-sequitous speech output (jumping between unrelated topics: inventory → Thursdays → church grill → boss's tone) without prior history of speech or language disorder. The acute onset in adulthood, absence of developmental language disorder history, lack of memory impairment, normal comprehension, normal motor function, and functional decline in work performance are consistent with primary progressive aphasia or other neurodegenerative process rather than a developmental language disorder. G31.83 (Primary progressive aphasia) better accounts for the acute adult-onset speech disorganization with preserved comprehension and cognition in other domains.
